query: For high-entropy alloys intended for demanding engineering applications, what testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs the retention or loss of toughness, and why? Specify a controlled change that would reveal the governing behavior, the predicted observations relative to a baseline, the boundaries within which the hypothesis should hold, prior evidence supporting it, and an outcome that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In single‐phase high‐entropy alloys, the degree of lattice distortion driven by atomic size mismatch controls the retention or loss of toughness. A moderate increase in lattice distortion enhances toughness by promoting beneficial dislocation interactions and nanoscale crack bridging, but excessive distortion triggers local chemical ordering and excessive lattice friction that impedes plasticity and reduces toughness.
generation.material_initial_state: A baseline high‐entropy alloy prepared with near‐equiatomic elemental ratios to minimize lattice distortion, featuring a homogeneous single‐phase microstructure.
generation.intervention: Systematically vary the alloy composition to increase the atomic size mismatch—by incorporating elements with larger or smaller atomic radii—while maintaining identical isothermal processing conditions to ensure single-phase formation.
generation.conditions: All alloys are synthesized under isothermal conditions ensuring a uniform single-phase structure and then tested at room temperature and at service-relevant elevated temperatures under controlled, identical conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Lattice distortion and the resultant local chemical order arising from atomic size mismatch.
generation.mechanism: A moderate degree of lattice distortion increases dislocation interactions and assists the formation of nanoscale crack bridges (a beneficial synergistic effect enhancing toughness). However, when distortion becomes too high, local chemical ordering develops and lattice friction excessively increases, which impedes dislocation mobility and results in reduced toughness.
generation.predicted_outcome: Compared to the baseline alloy, samples with a moderate increase in atomic size mismatch should display improved fracture toughness (potentially in the 15–30% range) due to enhanced plasticity and crack bridging, whereas alloys with excessive mismatch will show a drop in fracture toughness relative to the baseline.
generation.baseline: High-entropy alloy with low atomic size mismatch (minimal lattice distortion) serving as the toughness reference.
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies to single-phase high-entropy alloys synthesized under controlled isothermal conditions and may not hold in dual-phase or multiphase alloys where phase transformation mechanisms dominate. Testing is confined to room temperature and moderate elevation ranges relevant to engineering applications.
generation.uncertainty: The exact threshold of lattice distortion at which the transition from beneficial to detrimental effects on toughness occurs is not precisely determined and is expected to depend on the specific element combinations used; magnitude of toughness changes must be confirmed by further experimentation.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare a series of single-phase high-entropy alloys by systematically varying the elemental composition to incrementally increase atomic size mismatch. Conduct microstructural characterization (using XRD, TEM, and EDS) to quantify lattice distortion and assess the degree of local chemical ordering. Perform tensile and fracture toughness tests at both room temperature and elevated temperatures. Plot toughness as a function of measured lattice distortion.
measurements: Lattice parameters and distortion levels (via XRD and TEM)
Microstructural indicators of local chemical ordering
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the experiments show no non-monotonic (i.e., initially increasing then decreasing) relationship between lattice distortion and toughness—meaning either toughness does not improve at moderate distortion or continues to improve (or declines) without a turning point—the hypothesis that a critical level of lattice distortion governs toughness retention is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: We believe that the excellent strength, ductility and toughness of this high-entropy alloy results directly from this synergy of intrinsic (plasticity related) and extrinsic (shielding related) mechanisms, which (unlike traditional toughening mechanisms involving mainly precipitates and/or boundaries) primarily result from its special material characteristics of a low average SFE with possible variation of local SFE (that modulates the behaviour of full and partial dislocations locally), and high lattice friction (that provides strengthening from the increased resistance to the planar slip of dislocations and its influence on the motion of partial dislocations), the low SFE further contributing to the remarkable formation of nanoscale crack bridges within a few hundred nanometres of the crack tip. (Further deliberations on the controlling factors for this synergy of deformation mechanisms are described in Supplementary Note 3). In light of the unique nature of the origin of the tensile strength and ductility and the resulting excellent fracture toughness displayed by this high-entropy alloy, further optimization of these mechanisms may present new directions for the future design o

While the yield strength and KJIc fracture toughness of the medium-entropy CrCoNi and high-entropy CrMnFeCoNi alloys are comparable, the tensile strengths, tensile ductility and work of fracture of the CrCoNi alloy are significantly higher, by respectively ∼15, ∼30 and ∼50%, at room temperature. At cryogenic temperatures, the strengths of the two alloys are comparable (σUTS∼1,300 MPa at 77 K), but the KJIc fracture toughness, tensile ductility and work of fracture are again markedly higher in the CrCoNi alloy, by ∼25, ∼27 and ∼31%, respectively. The yield strength, σy, at 77 K is slightly below that of the CrMnFeCoNi alloy, which we believe is due to the non-uniform grain size of our present material (Fig. 1b–d). Consistent with this notion, in a previous study where the grain size of CrCoNi was uniform and comparable to that of the CrMnFeCoNi alloy, the tensile properties of the three-component alloy were found to exceed those of the five-component alloy at all temperatures.

chosen.why: This move directly addresses the open question by experimentally testing the hypothesis that the retention or loss of toughness is governed by the extent of lattice distortion (and associated local chemical order) driven by composition. By precisely altering the alloy composition while keeping processing variables constant, the study isolates the mechanistic role of atomic size mismatch. This approach is standard in the field and leverages well‐established synthesis and characterization techniques to reveal predicted variations in toughness relative to a baseline, thereby offering a clear outcome that would falsify the hypothesis if the expected correlations are absent.
